This indicates high statistical heterogeneity, as reflected by an I-squared value of 58%. Despite this inconsistency, all estimates suggest the same direction of effect. 2. Most trials included in the analysis were at high risk of bias for at least one domain, including incomplete outcome reporting (attrition bias), selective reporting (reporting bias), and publication bias. Additionally, all but one trial had unclear risk for random sequence generation and allocation concealment. 3. The total number of participants across all trials was 460. However, no data were reported for all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, stroke, myocardial infarction, end-stage renal disease, or heart failure events. 4. Event rates and sample sizes for each outcome were not included in the review. Baseline risk estimates were imputed from the incidence in a control group from a different systematic review. Events in the control arm were not provided. 5. The authors used the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) to assess study quality. The studies were a mix of high quality (27%), moderate quality (50%), and low quality (23%). Sensitivity analysis, including only high-quality trials, yielded results comparable to the overall analysis. 6. The upper end of the 95% CI crossed this threshold, suggesting the possibility of important harm. 8. Three large trials included in this comparison were not blinded, resulting in a high risk of performance and detection bias. Blinding was unclear in a fourth trial.
